description: We are Skorpe Monad, a multidisciplinary team passionate about space exploration, human health, open data and technology. Our skills span software development, design, research, data science and storytelling. We are exploring PROHOR, a prototype for understanding astronaut health data. We welcome a curious teammate interest​ed in space biology, healthcare, accessibility or software testing.
summary:
On a long-duration mission a crew member may have to judge a change in their own health while the flight surgeon is hours away. PROHOR is a local-first, offline-capable health workspace built for that moment. It records an indicator with its unit, compares it with that person's own earlier days a median and interquartile range over up to 30 distinct prior days and prints the sample count, the rule identifier and the source readings beside every flag. With fewer than seven usable prior days it reports insufficient prior data instead of implying reassurance.

Beside the workspace, an evidence explorer parses NASA's OSD-575 Inspiration4 serum metabolic panel in the browser: 531 observations, 19 analytes, four crew members, verified by SHA-256 and cited by source row number. Those rows are never a personal baseline and never a threshold. Four public feeds add dated Earth context — NASA DONKI, NOAA Kp, GOES proton flux, OSDR metadata — each showing its retrieval time and its fallback.

PROHOR exists because the dangerous failure in remote medicine is not missing data; it is a screen that says "red" without saying why, or "green" when nothing is known. Every flag here is reproducible from the readings printed next to it, and the handover packet — not the alert — is the product.
details:
PROHOR is a health workspace for the specific moment when a crew member is the only available assessor of their own condition. It is not an alert dashboard. It is an argument for a different design: publish your own evidence, refuse to score when you cannot, and hand the decision to a human.

source code, methodology, data provenance and the honest test report are in the public repository: https://github.com/tufayelahmedsuhagcc-dotcom/prohor

The Problem

On a long-duration mission the crew member records their own readings, decides whether a number matters, and acts — often with a delayed link to the ground. We studied how existing mission-health concepts answer that, and the failure mode that kept appearing is not a missing sensor. It is a colour. A badge that says "red" with no way to ask why pushes a crew member toward alarm fatigue; a badge that says "green" when nothing is known pushes them toward false reassurance. Both are decision errors, and both are invisible in a screenshot.

So PROHOR answers four questions, and every screen exists to answer one of them:

  1. What did I measure? — the value is entered with the unit that belongs to the indicator; nothing is imputed and nothing is silently converted.
  2. How does it compare with my own normal? — a personal baseline, never a population range.
  3. How much data supports that comparison? — window, sample count and data completeness are shown beside the flag, not behind a click.
  4. What do I do now? — one conservative routine step, and a structured handover for review.

1 Mission overview. Five indicators with their delta from the crew member's own median; the "5 indicators to review" banner opens the analysis instead of hiding it. Tagline in English and Bengali.

What The Prototype Does

Twelve indicators, eleven routed views, one working loop. A user can enter or import readings, watch a value enter their own baseline, see a change flagged with its arithmetic beside it, follow that flag into a routine prompt, and export a handover packet. Everything is computed in the browser from the data it claims to come from; there are no hard-coded display values.

  • Readings — typed entry, optional daily check-in, or atomic CSV import. Units are preserved and validated; invalid rows are rejected with a reason rather than dropped quietly.
  • Own-baseline comparison — median and interquartile range over up to 30 distinct prior days, excluding today's readings and any day without a valid value.
  • An honest floor — fewer than seven usable prior days means no comparison at all: the interface reports insufficient prior data. It never borrows a baseline from another crew member, another profile or another mode.
  • Inspectable evidence — window, sample count, rule identifier and the source readings sit beside every flag, and every chart has a table alternative with the same numbers.
  • Care plan — routine prompts tied to the flagged system, with done/deferred state kept per crew, day and mode. A prompt is a prompt; it is not a prescription.
  • Crew handover — the flagged readings, the baseline behind them, the routine step and free-text context, exported as a readable packet, as JSON, or printed to PDF. The handover, not the alert, is the deliverable.
  • Data sovereignty — import, restore, back up and erase. Erasure asks for confirmation and the export exists so nothing is trapped.
  • Health atlas — a coded schematic of six body systems, switchable between an anatomy and a skeleton layer, used purely as a map of what is measured. It states its own proxy limits: sleep and mood do not measure brain structure.
  • Offline — after the first visit the workspace runs from a service worker, with a labelled fallback for every feed.

2 Logging a reading. The unit belongs to the indicator, the measurement method is stated, and the save button says where the data goes: this device, no transmission.

3 Trends and baselines. The band is the median ± IQR over distinct prior days; the current value, the sample count and the rule sit beside it, and a table alternative carries the same numbers.

How It Works — Five Steps, None Of Which Reach A Server

  1. Entry. A value arrives with its indicator's unit attached by the interface, not guessed later.
  2. Store. It stays in this browser. Storage is unencrypted and single-device, and the product says so at the point of saving instead of in a policy page.
  3. Baseline. For the chosen indicator and profile, we take the latest valid reading from each distinct prior day inside the window and compute the median and interquartile range. Today is excluded. Future days are excluded. Missing values are excluded, and the excluded count is visible.
  4. Decide. A named, versioned rule — PROHOR-IQR-3.0 — compares the current value with that band using the indicator's direction (some indicators only matter when high, some only when low) and a change floor. The rule identifier is printed on the flag, so a reviewer can look it up.
  5. Review. A conservative routine step is proposed, and the case can be packaged for a human. No diagnosis, no dose, no fitness-for-duty call, at any point in the chain.

The design decision worth arguing about: a baseline is only honest if it says what it is made of. That is why the number of days, the sample count and the rule id travel with every flag instead of sitting in documentation. A brand-new local workspace therefore reports insufficient prior data — never a reassuring green. We consider that the feature.

4 Health atlas, anatomy layer. Six systems, each with its own flag state. The panel states the proxy limits: sleep and mood do not measure brain structure.

5 The same atlas in its skeleton layer — same systems, same readings, same flags; a second way to read the same map.

Nasa Data — What We Use, And What It Is Not

We use NASA's open science data for what it can actually support: a real, downloadable, hash-verifiable body of human spaceflight measurements, and the research context that tells us which indicators matter.

The NASA OSDR OSD-575 study (SpaceX Inspiration4, blood serum comprehensive metabolic panel and immune/cardiac cytokine arrays) is downloaded, hashed, and parsed in the browser. The evidence explorer compares 531 submitted observations across 19 analytes for the four crew members, shows collection time points (L-92 to R+82), and cites the source row number for every value it displays. The original submitted CSV and the transformed CSV ship with the app, so a reviewer can verify the SHA-256 of the exact bytes the interface parsed.

What the archive is not, and why we say so in the product: it is four people on a three-day flight with a handful of time points. It can illustrate a comparison; it cannot establish a long-mission threshold, and it never becomes anyone's personal baseline. Its rows are a separate, labelled research context with its own visual treatment. NASA HRP material — the five hazards, the sleep risk, the standard measures — is what we used to choose and frame the indicators, with links.

The same discipline applies to the sibling studies (OSD-569 whole blood, OSD-571 plasma, OSD-87 mouse retina). Metadata only, kept apart from human comparisons, cited rather than absorbed.

6 NASA evidence explorer. OSD-575 parsed in the browser: 531 observations, 19 analytes, four crew, source row numbers, hash-verified file.

Earth Context

Four feeds, one path each: bundled dated snapshot → same-origin adapter → schema validation → interface, with the observation time and the retrieval time both visible.

  • NASA DONKI notifications — the last 14 days of public space-weather notifications, typed, dated and linked. A log of what was reported, not a forecast and not a risk grade.
  • NOAA SWPC planetary K-index — live geomagnetic context, ten-minute cache, dated fallback.
  • NOAA GOES integral proton flux (>=10 MeV) — one sample per five-minute bucket, newest spacecraft only, shown as the particle environment near Earth. Explicitly not a dose and not a source of any threshold.
  • NASA OSDR study metadata — titles, descriptions and accession context for the studies above.

Cabin CO2 and any inside-the-spacecraft environment stays a separate, manual input. We could have implied that Earth-side geomagnetic data says something about the inside of a habitat. It does not, and the interface says so.

7 Space environment. Each feed names its source, its observation time and its retrieval time, and falls back to a dated snapshot when the network is unavailable.

Evidence That It Works

We would rather show numbers than adjectives, so here are the ones a reviewer can reproduce from the public repository:

  • 222 unit and adapter tests across 8 files, covering the rule engine, storage, CSV parsing, feed validation, the theme system and build invariants.
  • 225 browser assertions across five Playwright suites against the built app, including every one of the twelve panels at 320, 390 and 1440 px with a single h1 and no horizontal scrolling, and an assertion that no health record is ever POSTed anywhere.
  • 48 axe-core scans — twelve routes, two widths, light and dark — with zero violations under the WCAG 2.0/2.1 A and AA rule sets, under the shipped Content-Security-Policy.
  • 136 kB gzipped for the entire first load, and a 43-file / 0.98 MB offline install tier before the films and documents arrive in the background.
  • Byte-range playback verified online and offline: a real 206 for the demo film, from the cache when the network is gone.

The build is reproducible: npm ci && npm run build regenerates the exact committed output, and CI fails if the committed build differs from a fresh one.

Why There Is A Bengali Line

The hero greets the crew in Bengali — "মহাকাশে নিজের স্বাস্থ্য নিজে বুঝুন" ("understand your own health in space"). We are a five-person team from Sylhet, Bangladesh, and a crew member may well speak something other than English; a workspace that only speaks the language of the ground station is a small, real design failure. The Bengali subset is bundled locally (43 kB, SIL OFL), so it renders as text — not as empty boxes — on a machine with no Bengali font installed.

8 Crew handover. The flagged readings, the baseline behind them and the routine step, assembled into a packet a flight surgeon can read — printable, downloadable, never transmitted.

Tools And Technology

React 19 and TypeScript on Vite, with a deterministic analysis engine written as pure functions (no framework, no clock, no randomness) so it can be unit-tested and reasoned about. Zod validates every imported file and every feed response before it reaches the screen. PapaParse handles CSV both ways. Lucide provides icons. An Express adapter serves read-only public data locally and on Vercel, so the browser never talks to a third-party origin. A hand-written service worker implements the two-tier cache and byte-range video handling. Playwright and axe-core run the browser suites; Vitest runs the unit suites; the repo is MIT-licensed with a CI pipeline on GitHub Actions.

No runtime language model, no analytics, no trackers, no cookies, no account. The Content-Security- Policy is default-src 'self' with no third-party origin permitted for scripts, styles, fonts, images, media or connections — and it is enforced on the deployed site, not just described.

Creative Choices

Most health dashboards compete on how much they can infer. PROHOR competes on how much it can justify. Three consequences:

  • The uncertainty is the interface. Sample count, window and rule id are first-class elements, not tooltips. A reviewer can disagree with the rule and still follow it.
  • Refusal is a feature. "Insufficient prior data" and "unsupported range" are designed states with their own visual language, because the alternative — a calm-looking default — is the dangerous one.
  • The handover is the product. The alert is a means; a structured packet a flight surgeon can read in ninety seconds is the end. That reframing decided the information architecture of the whole app.

We also spent disproportionate time on the things that make a prototype feel real to a reviewer: dark mode re-derived rather than inverted, reduced-motion support, keyboard operation throughout, print styles that always use the light palette, a 320 px layout that is a real layout, and copy that never dresses a heuristic as a clinical finding.

Impact — Who This Is For, And What Changes

The immediate user is a crew member on a long-duration mission, and the second user is the flight surgeon who receives their handover. For the crew member, the change is that a bad day becomes explainable: what changed, against what baseline, with how much data, and what to do next. For the surgeon, the change is that the first five minutes of a delayed consultation stop being spent reconstructing what happened.

The same pattern — one person, far from a specialist, with a lag — is ordinary on Earth: rural clinics, expedition and ship medicine, disaster response, long-term care. The design is portable because it is just a browser and a local store, and we would like to test it there next. We have not tested it with astronauts, clinicians or patients; that is the gap between this prototype and a claim.

Responsible Limits

PROHOR is an independent research prototype, not a medical device. It does not diagnose, treat, prescribe, estimate radiation dose, determine fitness for duty, replace emergency procedures, or imply NASA endorsement. The baseline rule and its floors are documented heuristics and have not been clinically validated. The bundled mission records are synthetic and labelled as such in the interface; OSD-575 is separate historical research data and is never used as a threshold. Local storage is unencrypted, so it should not be used for identifiable medical information. Clinical review, privacy engineering and prospective validation would all be required before any operational use — and we would want that review to happen in that order.

Try It In 90 Seconds

  1. Open https://prohor.health — nothing to install, no account, no login.
  2. Follow the three steps under "One reading. A clearer story." on the overview.
  3. Open Trends & baselines and check the sample count and rule behind a flag against the readings printed beside it.
  4. Open NASA evidence and verify a value against its source row number.
  5. Open Crew handover and print the packet — that is the product.

Source code, methodology, data provenance and the honest test report are in the public repository: https://github.com/tufayelahmedsuhagcc-dotcom/prohor
